## Paper

## Abstract

Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) enables non-invasive analysis of transparent specimens across biomedicine, materials science, and neuroscience. However, conventional hardware relies on complex architectures with multi-shot acquisition that preclude compact, real-time operation, while phase-retrieval software often yields degraded image quality, is environmentally sensitive, and runs slowly. Here, we introduce a compact, fast, high-resolution QPI platform that addresses these challenges by integrating nanophotonic metasurfaces with artificial intelligence (AI). Our metasurface optics simplifies the optical architecture by replacing bulky optics and modulators, enabling single-shot acquisition and a drastic reduction in form factor. We develop physics-informed AI models that correct optical aberrations, compensate for imperfections in nanofabrication and alignment, and restore nanoscale quantitative phase information in real-time. The system achieves nanoscale resolution better than 840 nm at 74 Hz within a single, thin optical layer. Our unique combination of nanophotonic hardware and AI algorithms advances QPI technology towards portable, precise, real-time phase imaging.

---

## Introduction

The invention of the bright-field microscope in the 17th century revolutionized science by unlocking the exploration of the microscopic world through optical intensity1,2. Fritz Zernike’s development of phase contrast microscopy in the 1950s3, along with subsequent advancements4,5, enabled the observation of transparent and colorless specimens through the contrast or gradients of optical phase, revealing structures previously invisible to bright-field microscopes. While these methods provide valuable visualization, they remain at a qualitative level and lack precise, quantitative information about the optical properties and morphology of microscopic samples. Advanced applications require more accurate data, inspiring the development of quantitative phase imaging (QPI), which enables the quantitative visualization of optical phase. By offering non-invasive, label-free imaging, QPI has become indispensable across fields such as biomedical engineering, materials science, and neuroscience engineering, providing precise structural and functional information of microscopic samples critical to modern research6–8.

Emerging applications across various fields – from semiconductor inspection, in-vivo neuroimaging, and live cell bioimaging to nanometrology, mobile diagnostics, healthcare devices, and clinical microsurgery – demand compact, real-time QPI systems that deliver high-resolution, quantitative phase information without compromising system portability or acquisition speed. While there are various types of conventional QPI systems with different optical configurations and components, most remain far from miniaturization due to their reliance on interferometry or holography involving multi-element assemblies, relay optics, and long optical paths, resulting in substantial system bulk and complexity. Moreover, most of these systems require multi-shot measurements to capture the full light field information, utilizing additional opto-mechanical or electro-optical components such as piezo stages or spatial light modulators, which further increase system bulk, alignment sensitivity, and capture latency (Fig. 1a)9–11. Metasurface optics12–15 can enable system miniaturization with planar optics utilizing nanoscale light modulation capabilities in many applications, including augmented reality displays16,17, micro displays18, cameras19,20, image sensors21, endoscopy22,23, and phase contrast microscopy24–27. While promising, simplifying and miniaturizing QPI systems remains challenging due to the imperative need in QPI for sufficient degrees of freedom to complex light field reconstruction. Moreover, existing QPI methods are limited to low resolutions of only tens of microns, making them unsuitable for emerging nanotechnology applications, and they are susceptible to environmental disturbances and have long processing times7,28,29. While recent efforts have explored metasurface-assisted QPI using phase-only beam-splitting metasurface designs in combination with conventional or naive neural network-based reconstruction methods30,31, these systems still rely on bulky 4f architectures, and their algorithms have limited capability in phase retrieval, which significantly constrains their resolution, robustness, and potential for miniaturization. These challenges limit the development of real-time, portable, and precise QPI solutions, highlighting the demand for compact, high-performance optical systems coupled with precise and rapid reconstruction algorithms to unlock future applications in a variety of domains.

Here, we develop a QPI method that combines nanophotonic metasurface optics with artificial intelligence (AI)-driven algorithms to implement a compact QPI system with nanoscale resolution and real-time processing (Fig. 1b). Our system features a complex-amplitude metasurface32, which provides simultaneous nanoscale control over both the amplitude and phase of light, enabling single-shot measurements and nanoscale precision within a single-chip form factor. The precise complex-amplitude modulation at subwavelength scales provided by our metasurfaces simplifies microscope system configurations by eliminating the imperative need for complex interferometers or additional active components found in conventional systems, while maintaining competitive optical performance with optical aberration corrections. Computational algorithms have been developed for phase microscopy33–36, but previous approaches primarily focused on conventional bulk microscopes without accurate consideration of physics, limiting their scalability to miniaturized systems with complex physics. Furthermore, they are often limited to low resolutions of only tens of microns, making them unsuitable for emerging nanoscale applications, and they are typically susceptible to environmental disturbances and have long processing times, hindering practical applications. To address these challenges, we develop mathematical models that describe an aberration-corrected forward image formation and inverse phase retrieval within our miniaturized system by combining physical modeling and learnable AI components. The physics-informed training37,38 and experimentally captured datasets allow our models to account for system physics, hardware imperfections, and all optical phenomena in phase retrieval. Therefore, our AI-driven modeling approach, along with experimental datasets, provides high-quality QPI with fast processing times, enabling nanoscale and real-time QPI solutions within miniaturized systems. Our approach, combining nanophotonics and AI, represents a significant advance in optical engineering and machine learning for various application fields from life sciences to materials science.

---

## Results

Miniaturized microscopy with complex-amplitude metasurfaces
Conventional QPI systems traditionally rely on capturing multiple intensity images or interference patterns to reconstruct a quantitative phase image, necessitating complex, bulky optical setups such as interferometers10,39, 4f optical systems with spatial filtering40, and multi-illumination sources41–43, or additional opto-mechanical actuators or electro-optic modulators39,44, all of which pose fundamental bottlenecks for miniaturization. This is because QPI inherently requires capturing multiple degrees of freedom to reconstruct the full complex-amplitude field, requiring multi-shot or multiplexed measurements. To address these challenges, we propose a metasurface optical system that can collect sufficient light field information through a single-layer device with a single-shot measurement, fundamentally resolving the bottlenecks in miniaturized QPI systems.

We develop a multi-functional metasurface that integrates multiple optical functions within a single device (Fig. 2a). Based on the generalized law of refraction45, an off-axis metasurface lens (or metalens) can be designed to focus light at specific locations when the incident wavefront arrives at an oblique incident angle of θ. In addition, arbitrary optical aberrations can be introduced to the wavefront around the focal point by adding phase delays through the metasurface. By combining two different off-axis metalenses with distinct focal points and optical aberrations, our multi-functional metasurface can direct light from different incident angles to separate focal points, with each focus engineered to have specific optical aberrations or Zernike coefficients. This multiplexing of two off-axis metalenses is implemented by designing the complex-amplitude profile of the metasurface as the sum of the phase profiles of each metalens, each corresponding to a distinct focal position and aberration coefficient:

U(x,y) = \sum_{j} a(x_j,y_j) \cdot e^{ikt_j \cdot r} \cdot e^{i \sum_{m} a_{j,m} Z_m}

where U(x,y) represents the total complex-amplitude profile resulting from the superposition of multiple contributions indexed by j. Here, a(x_j,y_j) denotes the complex-amplitude profile of the metalens with a focal length at (x_j,y_j). The first exponential term introduces phase gradients for oblique incidence, with k as the transverse wave vector and r=(x,y) as the spatial coordinate vector. The second exponential term accounts for the additional wavefront aberrations, where a_{j,m} are coefficients modulating the m-th Zernike polynomial Z_m, typically used to model optical aberrations, including defocus. Figure 2a shows the amplitude and phase profile of the designed complex-amplitude profile U(x,y). This design enables the encoding of multiple optical functions into a single-layer metasurface, shrinking conventional bulk optical systems into a single planar device and eliminating the need for bulky interferometric components or additional modulators. Furthermore, the elimination of physical movement or wavefront modulation to measure multiple different intensity images enables single-shot measurements in our system.

To realize the multi-functional metasurface concept, we employ complex-amplitude metasurfaces composed of X-shaped silicon nanostructures, designed to simultaneously modulate the local amplitude and phase of visible light32. These X-shaped nanostructures allow control over the full range of both amplitude (from 0 to 1) and phase (from −π to π) by adjusting their shapes and orientations (see Methods for details). The subwavelength nanostructures, with a period of 330 nm, are designed to operate at a wavelength of 532 nm, enabling precise control over complex-amplitude fields and the modulation of high-spatial frequency components. We fabricate the metasurfaces using electron beam lithography (see Methods for details), and Fig. 2b, c show the fabricated metasurface sample and its corresponding scanning electron microscope (SEM) image.

Our design employs complex-amplitude metasurfaces rather than phase-only metasurfaces to implement multi-functional optical elements. While phase-only metasurfaces have been explored for multi-functionality24,46,47, their limited modulation capability restricts accurate reconstruction of complex-valued fields, resulting in fewer degrees of freedom for implementing multiple optical functions. In contrast, our complex-amplitude metasurface effectively suppresses phase conjugate replications and diffraction artifacts, while accurately implementing dual focal points with distinct Zernike coefficients to enhance coherent imaging quality. For baseline comparison, we also design and fabricate a phase-only metasurface, which shares the same phase profile as the complex-amplitude metasurface but maintains a unity amplitude profile across the aperture. Figure 2d, e show experimentally captured point spread functions of complex-amplitude and phase-only metasurfaces. The results demonstrate that our complex-amplitude metasurface significantly reduces diffraction artifacts caused by coherent interference between adjacent focal points. To further support this claim, we include additional experiments in Supplementary Fig. 3. These results show that diffraction artifacts from the phase-only metasurface degrade phase retrieval quality, whereas the cleaner intensity profiles enabled by the complex-amplitude metasurface lead to improved reconstruction accuracy and robustness across all reconstruction methods, which is especially beneficial for noise-sensitive applications like ours.

Quantitative phase retrieval with artificial intelligence
The proposed metasurface system can simultaneously capture multiple intensity images with distinct optical aberrations, so that a quantitative phase image can be reconstructed via a phase retrieval algorithm. Conventional phase retrieval algorithms, such as the transport-of-intensity equation (TIE)28, can reconstruct the phase profile ϕ(x,y,z) of a specimen from multiple intensity images captured at different depth planes or with different optical aberrations48. The conventional TIE algorithm is expressed as

k \frac{\partial I}{\partial z} = −\nabla_{xy} \cdot (I\nabla_{xy} \phi)

where I(x,y,z) represents the intensity and k is the wavenumber of the incident light. Despite their widespread use, conventional TIE methods have significant drawbacks, including resolution limitations, susceptibility to noise and artifacts, and difficulties in handling the physical complexities of more compact systems49,50. This makes them less suitable for our metasurface-based system, where coherent wavefront propagation is sensitive to factors including optical aberrations, nanophotonic effects, and nanofabrication imperfections. To overcome these challenges, we develop an AI-driven algorithm that combines physically accurate modeling and AI. The core idea of our approach is to design both a physically accurate microscopy image formation model (forward model) and a phase retrieval algorithm (inverse model), and also to calibrate learnable model components through physics-informed learning and experimentally captured datasets. Due to the absence of publicly available training datasets for QPI and its vulnerability to mismatches between theory and physical systems, relying solely on a single inverse model is insufficient for our applications compared to other applications in holography17,51,52 and computational photography53,54. The forward model enables the simulation of realistic intensity patterns, allowing the inverse model to learn accurate phase retrieval despite optical aberrations and nanoscale defects, providing better robustness and quality. This strategy ensures a deeper understanding of the system’s optical behavior.

The forward model simulates the coherent light propagation through the metasurface microscope system to produce intensity images at specific depth planes as input to the inverse retrieval model. Based on the angular spectrum method55, this model calculates the complex-valued point spread functions (PSFs) of the metasurface system at a particular depth z, which is expressed as

U_z = F^{-1} \{ F \{ U(x,y) \cdot u_{inc} \} \cdot H_z \}

where U(x,y) is the complex-amplitude profile of the metasurface, u_{inc} denotes the incident field, F is the Fourier transform, and H_z is the transfer function for wave propagation at a distance z. The resulting intensity image at depth z can be given by

I_z = | F^{-1} \{ F \{ a_{target} e^{i\phi_{target}} \} \cdot F \{ u_z \} \} |^2 + \eta

where a_{target} and ϕ_{target} denote the target amplitude and phase, and η ∼ N(0,σ^2) is the Gaussian read noise of an image sensor. These intensity images generated by the forward model are crucial for training the inverse model, allowing it to learn accurate mappings from intensity to phase by accounting for the physical system’s behavior.

While conventional TIE-based methods can serve as phase retrieval techniques, they are inadequate for our metasurface QPI system due to their reliance on paraxial approximations, poor handling of high-frequency information, and susceptibility to artifacts from noise and boundary conditions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce an AI-driven inverse model in the form of a convolutional neural network (CNN). Our phase retrieval network, denoted as CNN_{phase}, replaces the conventional TIE by directly converting intensity images into a phase map, bypassing the drawbacks of the traditional approaches. The inverse model can be expressed as

ϕ_{recon} = CNN_{phase}(I_0, I_z)

where I_0 and I_z are intensity images at different depth planes. The network is designed to reconstruct the phase ϕ_{recon}, also compensating for optical aberrations and noise that traditional solvers struggle with (see Supplements for details on training and network architecture). In addition, we augment this inverse model with a secondary correction network, CNN_{corr}, that is trained on experimental datasets to handle discrepancies between our forward model simulations and real-world experimental conditions, including further aberrations, nanofabrication mismatch, and nanoscale system misalignment. By leveraging both forward and inverse models, the system can learn a more accurate representation of the optical system behavior, enhancing the overall phase retrieval process.

Accurate and robust phase retrieval requires a reliable training process. We utilize a physics-informed loss function to guide the learning of our neural networks, ensuring that the reconstructed phase is consistent with the underlying physical principles. Rather than directly comparing phase images, which could lead to ambiguities due to phase offsets, our loss function considers free-space wavefront propagation by evaluating the discrepancies between diffraction patterns at multiple depth planes generated by the reconstructed and target phase maps (ϕ_{target} and ϕ_{recon}):

L(ϕ_{target}, ϕ_{recon}) = \sum_{i} || f_{free}(a_0 e^{i\phi_{target,z_i}}) |^2 - | f_{free}(a_0 e^{i\phi_{recon,z_i}}) |^2 ||^2

where f_{free} represents free-space propagation, z_i is a particular depth for each depth plane i, and a_0 is the amplitude profile at the target plane. By comparing multiple diffraction patterns rather than pixel-wise phase values, this physics-informed loss ensures physical accuracy while improving the network performance and mitigating artifacts like boundary inconsistencies and high-frequency blurring. The training process follows two steps: pre-training with synthetic datasets generated from the forward model, and refinement with experimentally captured datasets. In the pre-training stage, we generate synthetic intensity images using the forward microscopy model, simulating a variety of phase and amplitude distributions under realistic optical conditions, including Gaussian blur and practical constraints on amplitude-phase correlation (see “Methods” for details). This pre-training allows the network to generalize across a wide range of phase objects and handle various aberrations. Once pre-trained, the inverse model is refined with experimental datasets captured from our metasurface system, enabling it to adapt to practical conditions. During the capture refinement, the parameters of the initially trained CNN_{phase} are frozen, and only the parameters of CNN_{corr} are further trained to learn experimental environments. By freezing model parameters after initial pre-training on a large synthetic dataset, we reduce the amount of experimentally captured data required to sufficiently train our inverse model, which is beneficial in this application because both public availability and manual data collection are highly constrained. This approach, incorporating physics-informed learning and training on both synthetic and experimental datasets, enables our model to better understand underlying physical phenomena efficiently, resulting in more accurate, robust learning and superior visual quality compared to conventional methods.

Experimental results
We build an optical microscope setup with our metasurface to compare the performance of our phase retrieval models with existing approaches. The setup includes a coherent laser source with a wavelength of 532 nm, illumination optics, a fabricated metasurface, and a camera. Our metasurface can create two separate intensity images at different depths within a single image plane, allowing the camera to simultaneously capture two images with a single shot. To benchmark our method, we qualitatively and quantitatively assess the retrieved phase image quality and compare several different models: a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)-based direct TIE solver (TIE-Direct) offering fast processing at the cost of limited image quality, an iterative TIE solver (TIE-Iterative) with improved image quality but slow processing time and high sensitivity to optical aberrations, a non-physical inverse model with both physical and learned components but without physics-informed learning (see Supplements for details), and our physics-informed model with physics-informed learning. Note that the non-physical inverse model reflects the type of approach previously explored in deep learning-based QPI studies, which relied on naive forward models without physics-informed supervision or model calibration31,34. While the conventional TIE solvers are fundamentally limited in resolution and sensitive to experimental conditions, inverse models are expected to improve image quality with fast processing time. In particular, physics-informed learning procedures trained on experimental datasets are expected to enhance robustness to optical aberrations, system alignment, and nanofabrication defects, ultimately enabling better imaging performance.

Our initial experiments focus on assessing the performance of CNN_{phase}, initially trained with synthetic datasets generated from the forward microscopy model, using conventional microscopy setups. Figure 4 shows phase retrieval results from the intensity images with various methods. The existing TIE methods provide low image quality and suffer from background noise and artifacts, especially in the low-intensity region, where the solutions tend to diverge (see Supplements for detailed analysis of TIE solvers). In contrast, the inverse models show significant improvements by learning to compensate for aberrations and recover high-frequency details. This demonstrates that our physical modeling approach is effective in overcoming the resolution and robustness limitations of existing TIE methods and improving retrieval quality. In particular, the physics-based supervision enables very high-quality phase reconstruction through additionally supervising physical wave propagation.

Our compact metasurface microscope is composed of the fabricated metasurface with illumination optics and camera. Compared to conventional bulk microscopes, the compact metasurface microscope introduces more challenging conditions, with significantly increased optical aberrations, nanofabrication imperfections, and additional physical phenomena in nanophotonic devices. The correction CNN (CNN_{corr}) in the inverse model is designed to compensate for experiment mismatches and additional artifacts not accounted for in the forward model by refinement training with the experimental dataset captured through our compact metasurface microscope. Figure 5 shows the phase retrieval results, comparing the different inverse models. In all cases, our physics-informed inverse model outperforms baselines by a large margin. Our experimental results on the 1951 USAF resolution target further demonstrate the capability of our microscopy system to resolve element 2 in group 9, corresponding to a nanoscale spatial resolution of 870 nm or better. It is noteworthy that the image quality of the conventional TIE methods and the non-physical model is much worse than that using the conventional microscope in Fig. 4, due to more severe aberrations and additional artifacts caused by simplified design, imperfect nanofabrication, and nanophotonic phenomena of our metasurfaces. This highlights the strength of our approach in achieving robust, accurate phase retrieval even in the presence of complex system imperfections, which conventional methods fail to address, denoting our physics-informed supervision, along with experimental datasets, is inevitable for miniaturization and simplification of microscope systems.

We also demonstrate quantitative validation of our method compared to the others using custom target samples. As a ground truth phase object, we fabricate a custom-designed metasurface target with step-like phase regions defined by 3.10 μm features, equivalent to group 7, element 3 of a standard USAF 1951 target. This target manipulates local phase delay by engineering the effective refractive index of its nanostructures, making it physically equivalent to traditional stepped-height references (see Supplementary Note 3 for details). Figure 5c, d demonstrate that our model can recover quantitative phase information more accurately than other methods (see Supplements for a detailed quantitative comparison of reconstructed phase values). For real-time applications, we also measure the runtime of each method to see how fast our model is compared to others. Our model, with very high performance and robustness, offers fast processing times of 13.5 ms per frame or, similarly, 74 Hz, making it suitable for real-time applications. Notably, our method, based on single-shot measurement, has no additional latency other than computing runtime since the system measures multiple intensity images simultaneously. However, other methods based on multi-shot measurements incur additional time delay between measurements on top of the computational runtime, highlighting the rapid speed of our approach.

## Methods

Metasurface design with X-shaped meta-atoms
To realize the proposed concept of the multi-functional metalens with two focal points with distinct Zernike coefficients, we design the complex amplitude profiles by summing two different complex amplitude profiles of off-axis metalenses with different focal positions and coefficients as expressed in Eq. (1). Figure 2 depicts the amplitude and phase profiles of the designed complex metasurfaces, which have a focal length of 1 mm for both two focal points. In this design, a Zernike defocus coefficient corresponding to the depth of 3 μm is added to one of the two focal points, and the phase gradients with the transverse wave vector of k_t = k_0 sin(θ) are designed such that each focal point has the separation angle (θ) of ±4°, respectively.

To implement the complex-amplitude metasurface, we utilize an X-shaped metasurface to manipulate complex-amplitude profiles on a subwavelength scale32. As an extension of the Pancharatnam–Berry phase principle, the X-shaped meta-atom allows for a full range of both amplitude and phase to be mapped and adjusted by tuning the orientation angles of its two arms. The X-shaped meta-atom can be modeled as two independent electric dipoles, and its behavior can be analyzed by the superposition of the geometric phase. The complex-amplitude modulation of X-shaped meta-atoms can be expressed as

E_{cross} / 2 cos(θ_1 - θ_2) exp(j(θ_1 + θ_2))

where θ_1 and θ_2 are the orientation angles of two arms consisting of the X-shaped structure and σ represents the handedness of the circular polarization. The adjustment of the two orientation angles of rods enables simultaneous modulation of amplitude and phase. The phase component of the cross-polarized component is proportional to the sum of their orientation angles, while the amplitude component is proportional to the cosine of the differences between their orientation angles. In this work, the X-shaped meta-atom is composed of hydrogenated amorphous-silicon (a-Si:H) with a period of 330 nm, which is smaller than the operating wavelength of 532 nm for satisfying Nyquist sampling theory (see Supplements for details).

Metasurface sample fabrication
We use electron beam lithography to fabricate our metasurface, as depicted in Supplementary Fig. 9. First, amorphous silicon (a-Si) with a thickness of 150 nm is deposited onto a glass wafer using plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) (HiDep-SC, BMR Technology). Then, positive e-beam resists PMMA 495 A4 and PMMA 950 A2 are spin-coated on the a-Si layer. Conductive polymer (E-spacer 300Z) is also coated to prevent charge accumulation. Our metasurface is patterned using an electron beam lithography (JBX-6300FS, JEOL), followed by developing of sample with a MIBK/IPA 1:3 developer. A chromium (Cr) layer with a thickness of 20 nm is deposited as a hard mask using electron beam evaporation (KVE-3004, Korea Vacuum Tech). The resists are removed using acetone, followed by etching the a-Si layer using an inductively coupled plasma (ICP) etcher (Multiplex ICP, STS). Finally, the Cr hard mask is removed using a Cr etchant.

Experimental measurements
Our experimental setups are designed to evaluate the performance of our metalens and quantitative phase imaging (QPI). Two experiments are conducted: measuring the point spread function (PSF) and demonstrating QPI. The experimental setup depicted in Supplementary Fig. 10 is utilized for the PSF measurements. The monochrome laser with a wavelength of 532 nm consists of supercontiuum laser source (SuperK, NKT Photonics) with a monochromator are utilized as a light source. This light passes through a cascaded linear polarizer and quarter waveplate for the generation of circular polarization as an input for our metalens. An objective lens (MPlanFLN, 50×, NA=0.8, Olympus) captures two PSFs of our metalens and is then focused by a tube lens (f=50 mm, Nikon). Next, a cascaded quarter waveplate and linear polarizer is inserted for capturing only cross-polarized light. The PSFs are finally captured with charge-coupled device (CCD) camera (Blackfly S BFS-U3-120S4C, Color, pixel pitch of 1.85 μm, FLIR).

The QPI demonstration is based on a setup depicted in Supplementary Fig. 11. The same light source and polarization components are utilized. An objective lens (MPlanFLN, 5×, NA=0.15, Olympus) is used as a condenser lens for focusing light to the samples. Then, our metalens acts as an objective lens and separate two-depth images. The same tube lens (f=50 mm, Nikon) and polarization components are inserted as in the PSF measurement. Two images are finally captured with a CCD camera (Blackfly S BFS-U3-17S7C-C, Color, pixel pitch of 9 μm, FLIR).

For the conventional experimental demonstration, a standard microscopy system is utilized. The laser-line filtered LED is utilized as a light source. The sample image is magnified with an objective lens (MPlanFLN, 50×, NA=0.8, Olympus) and a tube lens of 180 mm focal length. The image is captured with a CCD camera (Blackfly S BFS-U3-17S7C-C, Color, pixel pitch of 9 μm, FLIR).

Synthetic dataset for pre-training
A set of random phase data is generated by using Equations (7), (8), and (9) as simulated targets. Equation (7) represents a two-dimensional Gaussian function utilized for blurring. In this equation, m and n denote the coordinates of a pixel in 2D space, while R denotes a single random variable that governs the radius of the Gaussian functions. In addition, A represents the normalization constant used to ensure that the summation of Gaussian functions equals to 1.

g(m,n) = A exp(-(m^2+n^2)/R^2)

Y(m,n) = g(m,n) * X(m,n)

φ(m,n) = ϕ_0 tanh(2βY(m,n) - β) / tanh(2β)

X(m,n) in Equation (8) represents a random matrix where each component is independent and follows a uniform distribution in the range of [0,1]. This equation applies a Gaussian blur to the original random matrix. The * operation here denotes a convolution operator. By convolving the original data with a Gaussian function, we effectively blur or smooth the data into Y(m,n). Equation (9) finally generates the random phase data while considering physical constraints. The blurred data Y(m,n) undergoes the hyperbolic tangent function, where the parameter β controls the sharpness of the generated phase. Higher values of β result in sharper contrast. The examples of the random phase data are plotted in Supplementary Fig. 7.

Neural network architecture and training details
We use the U-net architecture for the learnable components in our models, noted for its proficiency in complex image reconstruction tasks, which is particularly advantageous for our phase-retrieval application. The details of the CNNs are explained in the Supplement. For the loss function, we employ an L1 loss function of intensity generated from the recovered phase using a free-space propagation model. The Adam optimizer is employed with a learning rate of 1e-4 for training the phase retrieval network. During training, a batch size of 4 is used, with each epoch consisting of 100 synthetic phase datasets. It is noteworthy that each epoch uses a distinct dataset to promote variation in training. The dimensions of the input data for intensity are 480 × 480. In addition, Gaussian noise with a standard deviation between 0 and 0.01 is included in the training data. The training is conducted on a system running Ubuntu, equipped with Intel Xeon(R) CPU E5-2698 and NVIDIA Tesla V100.

For pre-training, we use the synthetic dataset to produce network training data using the forward image formation model (Fig. 3a). Two point spread functions (PSFs) of our complex-amplitude metasurface are first simulated with the angular spectrum method (ASM). Before the convolution with the PSFs, the normalized amplitudes are combined with the randomly generated phase maps, creating the complex amplitude fields. The complex amplitudes are padded with 3 times of their original size using the replicate padding method. Subsequently, the padded complex amplitudes are convolved with two PSFs utilizing fast Fourier transform (FFT), and the central region is cropped with its original size. We apply an absolute-value-square operator for both cropped images to calculate the simulated intensity images, which are next normalized to have a maximum intensity of 1, maintaining the scale between two images. To account for the Gaussian read noise of an image sensor, η ∼ N(0,σ^2) is added to the intensity images, where σ is 0.01. These processed images are utilized as input data for training the phase retrieval network (CNN_{phase}). For the physics-informed supervision, We also pad the recovered output phase of the neural network image and propagate the padded data using the ASM before cropping it. In addition, we evaluate the loss on the intensity obtained from the absolute square of the propagated wavefronts. After the pre-training, the refinement procedure (Fig. 3b) trains the correction network (CNN_{corr}) with experimentally captured datasets through our inverse model with physics-informed learning, while the pre-trained parameters of the phase retrieval network (CNN_{phase}) are fixed. The experimental dataset contains intensity images at different depth planes captured by the metasurface microscope system, consisting of two intensity images obtained at the off-axis focal points of the proposed complex-amplitude metasurface and additional intensity images obtained via on-axis mechanical translation of the metasurface microscope system for further training data. Both the on-axis and off-axis intensity images are used in the capture refinement procedure. On-axis images have higher phase retrieval quality than off-axis images due to the smaller offset between intensity pairs, which increases the upper bound on the retrieval results of the inverse model during refinement (see Supplements for details).

Unlike other AI applications17,35,51–54, our application for nanoscale QPI makes it much more challenging to adopt AI in terms of dataset generation, given the difficulty in accurately and massively capturing quantitative phase information of microscopic samples at the nanoscale resolution. Our subsequent learning method with both synthetic and experimental datasets can alleviate the burden on the size of the experimentally captured dataset, enabling sufficient model training with a minimized experimental dataset size.

Sample preparation
For the QPI demonstrations shown in Figs. 4 and 5, we utilized a USAF 1951 resolution chart (Edmund Optics), and onion samples purchased from a grocery store. The phase samples used as ground truth in Fig. 5 are prepared through only a part of the E-beam lithography process. For the PMMA metasurface with rectangular holes, PMMA 495 A4 is applied by spin-coating onto a silicon nitride (SiN) on glass substrate. The patterning is accomplished via E-beam lithography, and then the MIBK/IPA 1:3 developer is utilized for development. Supplementary Fig. 15d displays a scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image of the fabricated ground-truth sample. The pixel pitch of the PMMA metasurface is 350 nm. The refractive index of PMMA 495 A4 at 532 nm wavelength, as stated in the datasheet, is roughly 1.49. The height of the PMMA layer is measured to be approximately 350 nm through SEM. Supplementary Fig. 15a displays the amplitude and phase modulation in relation to width, simulated using the rigorous coupled-wave analysis68.

Image Template Matching for Pre-processing
For the results captured through our metasurface in Figs. 4 and 5, we use image template matching to crop identical areas from two depth images in a single image plane, as described in

R(m,n) = \sum_{i,j} X(i,j) Y(i+m, j+n)

We fix one image’s (X) crop window position and roughly estimate the initial position of the other image’s (Y) crop window. By shifting Y by (m,n) pixels, we calculate the cross-correlation (R) of the two images. The location where R reaches its maximum is identified as the best match, and the cropping window of Y is aligned accordingly. When using a single image captured by the metalens through conventional z-stage translation, the identical crop windows are applied to both depth images. Additional details can be found in the Supplements.

Conventional phase retrieval algorithms
The phase retrieval algorithms utilized in Figs. 4 and 5 include the FFT-based direct TIE and iterative TIE. For the direct TIE, we utilize the method developed by Paganin and Nugent69. The solution of direct TIE can be expressed as

ϕ(x) = -k \nabla^{-2} \nabla \cdot ( \frac{1}{I(x)} \nabla \nabla^{-2} \frac{\partial I}{\partial z} )

where an inverse Laplacian ∇^{-2} can be translated into the Fourier domain by the equation ∇^{-2} = 1 / (4π^2 |u|^2). This enables utilizing the FFT computationally for rapid phase reconstruction. In this method, the FFT necessitates a periodic boundary condition. Due to 1/I(x), the solution would diverge when I has many near zero components.

For the iterative TIE, we use the iterative method developed by Zhang et al.70. This iteration-based algorithm can be expressed as

ϕ(x) = -k \nabla^{-2} ( \frac{1}{I_{max}} \frac{\partial I}{\partial z} )

which assumes uniform intensities. The retrieved phase from this equation is utilized to determine the discrepancy of the intensity derivative through TIE or angular spectrum method. Based on this, the correction term for the phase is derived using the preceding equation and iteratively converged to the optimized phase profile. This iterative method typically outperforms the direct TIE method due to its applicability to inhomogeneous boundary conditions and near-zero components.

Quantitative analysis
The quantitative analysis presented in Fig. 5 utilizes root mean square error (RMSE) and structural similarity index measure (SSIM) to compare the recovered phase image with the ground-truth phase template. Unlike intensity images, phase images can differ by an unknown constant offset while still conveying the same structural information. Accordingly, the same RMSE and SSIM formulas used for the intensity images are applied, but evaluated after adding a global phase offset to the recovered phase image so that RMSE is minimized and SSIM is maximized. Mathematically, the RMSE and SSIM can be expressed as

RMSE = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{MN} \sum_{i=1}^{M} \sum_{j=1}^{N} (ϕ(i,j) - (ϕ_{gt}(i,j) + ϕ_c))^2 }

SSIM(x,y) = (2μ_x μ_y + c_1)(2σ_{xy} + c_2) / ((μ_x^2 + μ_y^2 + c_1)(σ_x^2 + σ_y^2 + c_2))

where the additive phase constant ϕ_c are determined to minimize RMSE and maximize SSIM. In addition, x and y denote the corresponding coordinates in the recovered phase image and the ground-truth image, respectively, within a window of size 11 × 11. Here, μ_x and μ_y are the average values of window x and y, respectively. Also, σ_x^2 and σ_y^2 are the variance of the windows x and y, respectively, and σ_{xy} is the covariance of the windows x and y, respectively.

These limitations would make the approach challenging to implement in reflection mode or with general objects that don't satisfy the weak phase approximation. robustness. For example, recent lensfree QPI implementations illustrate these limitations.

scanning with laser illumination, requiring a long source-to-sample distance, precision actuator

Figure 3), which degrade phase reconstruction across all methods, including baseline

suppresses these artifacts, producing cleaner intensity distributions and significantly improved

reconstruction method depends directly on the captured intensity images, improvements in raw

We respectfully disagree with the reviewer’s assertion that our work is limited due to its use of
coherent illumination or a reliance on the weak-phase approximation. In addition, we also
disagree with the implication that other metasurface-based QPI approaches operate under
incoherent illumination. This comment appears to reflect a misunderstanding of both the
fundamental requirements of quantitative phase imaging (QPI) and the capabilities of our
proposed method.
First, the suggestion that metasurface-based systems should preferentially operate under
incoherent illumination overlooks a central point: quantitative phase imaging fundamentally
requires coherence. The vast majority of QPI techniques—regardless of whether they use
conventional optics or metasurfaces—depend on either coherent or partially coherent
illumination to extract phase information. This includes established methods such as TIE
microscopy (Phys. Rev. Lett. 1998; DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.80.2586, Opt. Lasers Eng. 2020;
DOI: 10.1016/j.optlaseng.2020.106233), digital holography (Opt. Lett. 1999; DOI:
10.1364/OL.24.000291, Opt. Lett. 2005; DOI: 10.1364/OL.30.000468, Light Sci. Appl. 2024;
DOI: 10.1038/s41377-024-01453-x), Fourier ptychographic microscopy (Nat. Photonics 2013;
DOI: 10.1038/nphoton.2013.187), and many more technologies (Nat. Photon 2018;
DOI:10.1038/s41566-018-0253-x). Even recent metasurface-integrated QPI systems are all
demonstrated under coherent sources (Nat. Photonics 2020; DOI: 10.1038/s41566-019-0536-x,
Nano Lett. 2025; DOI: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c06039, ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2025; DOI:
10.1021/acsami.5c02901). These examples confirm that the requirement for coherence is not a
limitation of our specific approach, but a universal physical prerequisite for QPI across all optical
platforms. By contrast, imaging under fully incoherent illumination cannot support quantitative
phase retrieval, as it lacks the phase correlations needed to infer optical path length differences.
While incoherent illumination can be advantageous in general-purpose imaging (e.g., for
eliminating speckle in fluorescent or bright-field modalities), it is inherently incompatible with the
goals of QPI. Thus, it is incorrect to frame incoherent illumination as an advantage in this
context.
Second, we clarify that our approach is not restricted to weak-phase objects. This assumption is
often necessary in traditional analytical TIE methods, but our framework does not rely on the
weak-phase or paraxial approximations. Instead, we employ a physics-informed deep learning
model trained on both simulated and experimentally captured datasets. This model directly
learns the nonlinear forward and inverse mappings between intensity images and phase
profiles, effectively overcoming the limitations of conventional TIE by the paraxial
approximations. As a result, our method enables robust phase retrieval even in the presence of
large phase variations, moderate scattering, and severe optical aberrations in compact,
integrated systems. As demonstrated in Figure 5 of the manuscript, our method successfully
reconstructs complex biological samples that contain significant phase variations across both
intracellular and extracellular regions. These samples clearly exceed the weak-phase regime,
yet our approach recovers high-quality phase maps with accurate morphological features and
strong biological interpretability. Furthermore, we have added 3D visualizations (Supplementary
Figures 21–23) that emphasize these spatial variations, reinforcing that our system is capable of
handling a wide range of phase distributions.
Third, while interferometric QPI methods can be difficult to scale to compact or reflection-mode
geometries due to coherence requirements and alignment sensitivity, our metasurface-based
TIE framework is inherently more flexible. TIE is known to be highly tolerant of partial
coherence, and can be implemented using spatially incoherent but temporally coherent sources
such as LED arrays. This makes it one of the most adaptable phase imaging techniques
available for compact hardware integration. For example, as described in Opt. Lasers Eng. 2020
(DOI: 10.1016/j.optlaseng.2020.106233), TIE can operate effectively under low-coherence
illumination conditions that are incompatible with full-field holography or interferometry.
In summary, the reviewer’s concern about the coherence requirement and weak-phase
limitations does not reflect the physical realities of QPI or the actual capabilities of our system.
Our approach uses coherence in a way that is consistent with all mainstream QPI methods,
while offering increased tolerance to system imperfections and flexibility in implementation.
Importantly, our work fully leverages the unique benefits of metasurfaces—including
multi-functionality, complex-amplitude modulation, and compact integration—to enable an
optical platform that is both scalable and high-performing. The framework is not restricted to
weak-phase objects and remains applicable to real-world imaging scenarios involving strong
phase gradients and moderate scattering, making it broadly useful across biological and
biomedical applications.
---
Again, we appreciate the constructive feedback of all reviewers and have revised our
manuscript and supplement to clarify all of these comments.
Thank you very much for your consideration,

This reviewer appreciates the authors' efforts in revising the manuscript, including the addition of new supplementary notes, expanded experimental validation, and clarification of technical details. The revised manuscript shows improvement in presentation and addresses several reviewers' concerns. However, this reviewer still has reservations about several fundamental aspects of this work.
Most concerning is the fundamental limitation revealed in the authors' response regarding linear phase ramps. Since linear phase ramps constitute the Fourier basis for arbitrary optical fields, the inability to accurately measure any of these components would imply that the system cannot accurately reconstruct complex phase patterns with different spatial frequencies. The authors claim their TIE-based approach can detect such gradients through the edge intensity variation term ∇I·∇ϕ, but this argument is not correct. For a uniform beam with a linear phase ramp, the intensity gradient ∇I equals zero throughput the bulk of the field, meaning that most of the field provides no phase information. This differs fundamentally from interferometric quantitative phase methods that directly measure phase across the entire field.
The mathematical implications of this edge-only measurement approach are significant. Recovering a global phase profile from boundary information alone constitutes an ill-posed problem, where multiple different phase distributions could produce identical edge intensity patterns. This makes the reconstruction highly sensitive to noise and boundary conditions, with small errors at edges propagating throughout the entire reconstructed phase map. Since the system cannot reliably measure any of these fundamental Fourier basis functions across the field, it cannot accurately measure complex phase patterns with different spatial frequencies. The authors' attempt to minimize this issue by labeling it a "field of view limitation" rather than acknowledging it as a fundamental measurement limitation may not fully capture the nature of this constraint. Unlike their system, interferometric and holographic QPI methods can accurately reconstruct linear gradients throughout their field of view, not just at boundaries.
While the authors provide extensive arguments defending their metasurface choice over holographic optical elements, their comparison would benefit from a more balanced perspective. They emphasize HOE limitations such as Bragg selectivity and fabrication constraints while understating comparable metasurface challenges, including the need to maintain sub 100 nm feature uniformity across large areas and the associated fabrication costs. The claim that HOEs cannot achieve complex amplitude modulation could be better substantiated, as modern computer-generated HOEs have demonstrated sophisticated modulation capabilities.
The validation of quantitative phase accuracy remains insufficient. The authors' custom phase target consists exclusively of high-frequency diffractive structures implemented as varying nanohole arrays, rather than traditional stepped-height references. This approach only demonstrates accuracy for phase patterns with high spatial frequencies. Notably absent is any validation using uniform height steps in standard phase target that are characteristic of biological samples. Without testing against standard commercial phase targets or fabricated height steps of known dimensions, the claim of quantitative accuracy for general phase imaging applications remains unsubstantiated.

## Paper

## Abstract

Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) enables non-invasive analysis of transparent specimens across biomedicine, materials science, and neuroscience. However, conventional hardware relies on complex architectures with multi-shot acquisition that preclude compact, real-time operation, while phase-retrieval software often yields degraded image quality, is environmentally sensitive, and runs slowly. Here, we introduce a compact, fast, high-resolution QPI platform that addresses these challenges by integrating nanophotonic metasurfaces with artificial intelligence (AI). Our metasurface optics simplifies the optical architecture by replacing bulky optics and modulators, enabling single-shot acquisition and a drastic reduction in form factor. We develop physics-informed AI models that correct optical aberrations, compensate for imperfections in nanofabrication and alignment, and restore nanoscale quantitative phase information in real-time. The system achieves nanoscale resolution better than 840 nm at 74 Hz within a single, thin optical layer. Our unique combination of nanophotonic hardware and AI algorithms advances QPI technology towards portable, precise, real-time phase imaging.

---

## Introduction

The invention of the bright-field microscope in the 17th century revolutionized science by unlocking the exploration of the microscopic world through optical intensity1,2. Fritz Zernike’s development of phase contrast microscopy in the 1950s3, along with subsequent advancements4,5, enabled the observation of transparent and colorless specimens through the contrast or gradients of optical phase, revealing structures previously invisible to bright-field microscopes. While these methods provide valuable visualization, they remain at a qualitative level and lack precise, quantitative information about the optical properties and morphology of microscopic samples. Advanced applications require more accurate data, inspiring the development of quantitative phase imaging (QPI), which enables the quantitative visualization of optical phase. By offering non-invasive, label-free imaging, QPI has become indispensable across fields such as biomedical engineering, materials science, and neuroscience engineering, providing precise structural and functional information of microscopic samples critical to modern research6–8.

Emerging applications across various fields – from semiconductor inspection, in-vivo neuroimaging, and live cell bioimaging to nanometrology, mobile diagnostics, healthcare devices, and clinical microsurgery – demand compact, real-time QPI systems that deliver high-resolution, quantitative phase information without compromising system portability or acquisition speed. While there are various types of conventional QPI systems with different optical configurations and components, most remain far from miniaturization due to their reliance on interferometry or holography involving multi-element assemblies, relay optics, and long optical paths, resulting in substantial system bulk and complexity. Moreover, most of these systems require multi-shot measurements to capture the full light field information, utilizing additional opto-mechanical or electro-optical components such as piezo stages or spatial light modulators, which further increase system bulk, alignment sensitivity, and capture latency (Fig. 1a)9–11. Metasurface optics12–15 can enable system miniaturization with planar optics utilizing nanoscale light modulation capabilities in many applications, including augmented reality displays16,17, micro displays18, cameras19,20, image sensors21, endoscopy22,23, and phase contrast microscopy24–27. While promising, simplifying and miniaturizing QPI systems remains challenging due to the imperative need in QPI for sufficient degrees of freedom to complex light field reconstruction. Moreover, existing QPI methods are limited to low resolutions of only tens of microns, making them unsuitable for emerging nanotechnology applications, and they are susceptible to environmental disturbances and have long processing times7,28,29. While recent efforts have explored metasurface-assisted QPI using phase-only beam-splitting metasurface designs in combination with conventional or naive neural network-based reconstruction methods30,31, these systems still rely on bulky 4f architectures, and their algorithms have limited capability in phase retrieval, which significantly constrains their resolution, robustness, and potential for miniaturization. These challenges limit the development of real-time, portable, and precise QPI solutions, highlighting the demand for compact, high-performance optical systems coupled with precise and rapid reconstruction algorithms to unlock future applications in a variety of domains.

Here, we develop a QPI method that combines nanophotonic metasurface optics with artificial intelligence (AI)-driven algorithms to implement a compact QPI system with nanoscale resolution and real-time processing (Fig. 1b). Our system features a complex-amplitude metasurface32, which provides simultaneous nanoscale control over both the amplitude and phase of light, enabling single-shot measurements and nanoscale precision within a single-chip form factor. The precise complex-amplitude modulation at subwavelength scales provided by our metasurfaces simplifies microscope system configurations by eliminating the imperative need for complex interferometers or additional active components found in conventional systems, while maintaining competitive optical performance with optical aberration corrections. Computational algorithms have been developed for phase microscopy33–36, but previous approaches primarily focused on conventional bulk microscopes without accurate consideration of physics, limiting their scalability to miniaturized systems with complex physics. Furthermore, they are often limited to low resolutions of only tens of microns, making them unsuitable for emerging nanoscale applications, and they are typically susceptible to environmental disturbances and have long processing times, hindering practical applications. To address these challenges, we develop mathematical models that describe an aberration-corrected forward image formation and inverse phase retrieval within our miniaturized system by combining physical modeling and learnable AI components. The physics-informed training37,38 and experimentally captured datasets allow our models to account for system physics, hardware imperfections, and all optical phenomena in phase retrieval. Therefore, our AI-driven modeling approach, along with experimental datasets, provides high-quality QPI with fast processing times, enabling nanoscale and real-time QPI solutions within miniaturized systems. Our approach, combining nanophotonics and AI, represents a significant advance in optical engineering and machine learning for various application fields from life sciences to materials science.

---

## Results

Miniaturized microscopy with complex-amplitude metasurfaces
Conventional QPI systems traditionally rely on capturing multiple intensity images or interference patterns to reconstruct a quantitative phase image, necessitating complex, bulky optical setups such as interferometers10,39, 4f optical systems with spatial filtering40, and multi-illumination sources41–43, or additional opto-mechanical actuators or electro-optic modulators39,44, all of which pose fundamental bottlenecks for miniaturization. This is because QPI inherently requires capturing multiple degrees of freedom to reconstruct the full complex-amplitude field, requiring multi-shot or multiplexed measurements. To address these challenges, we propose a metasurface optical system that can collect sufficient light field information through a single-layer device with a single-shot measurement, fundamentally resolving the bottlenecks in miniaturized QPI systems.

We develop a multi-functional metasurface that integrates multiple optical functions within a single device (Fig. 2a). Based on the generalized law of refraction45, an off-axis metasurface lens (or metalens) can be designed to focus light at specific locations when the incident wavefront arrives at an oblique incident angle of θ. In addition, arbitrary optical aberrations can be introduced to the wavefront around the focal point by adding phase delays through the metasurface. By combining two different off-axis metalenses with distinct focal points and optical aberrations, our multi-functional metasurface can direct light from different incident angles to separate focal points, with each focus engineered to have specific optical aberrations or Zernike coefficients. This multiplexing of two off-axis metalenses is implemented by designing the complex-amplitude profile of the metasurface as the sum of the phase profiles of each metalens, each corresponding to a distinct focal position and aberration coefficient:

U(x,y) = \sum_{j} a(x_j,y_j) \cdot e^{ikt_j \cdot r} \cdot e^{i \sum_{m} a_{j,m} Z_m}

where U(x,y) represents the total complex-amplitude profile resulting from the superposition of multiple contributions indexed by j. Here, a(x_j,y_j) denotes the complex-amplitude profile of the metalens with a focal length at (x_j,y_j). The first exponential term introduces phase gradients for oblique incidence, with k as the transverse wave vector and r=(x,y) as the spatial coordinate vector. The second exponential term accounts for the additional wavefront aberrations, where a_{j,m} are coefficients modulating the m-th Zernike polynomial Z_m, typically used to model optical aberrations, including defocus. Figure 2a shows the amplitude and phase profile of the designed complex-amplitude profile U(x,y). This design enables the encoding of multiple optical functions into a single-layer metasurface, shrinking conventional bulk optical systems into a single planar device and eliminating the need for bulky interferometric components or additional modulators. Furthermore, the elimination of physical movement or wavefront modulation to measure multiple different intensity images enables single-shot measurements in our system.

To realize the multi-functional metasurface concept, we employ complex-amplitude metasurfaces composed of X-shaped silicon nanostructures, designed to simultaneously modulate the local amplitude and phase of visible light32. These X-shaped nanostructures allow control over the full range of both amplitude (from 0 to 1) and phase (from −π to π) by adjusting their shapes and orientations (see Methods for details). The subwavelength nanostructures, with a period of 330 nm, are designed to operate at a wavelength of 532 nm, enabling precise control over complex-amplitude fields and the modulation of high-spatial frequency components. We fabricate the metasurfaces using electron beam lithography (see Methods for details), and Fig. 2b, c show the fabricated metasurface sample and its corresponding scanning electron microscope (SEM) image.

Our design employs complex-amplitude metasurfaces rather than phase-only metasurfaces to implement multi-functional optical elements. While phase-only metasurfaces have been explored for multi-functionality24,46,47, their limited modulation capability restricts accurate reconstruction of complex-valued fields, resulting in fewer degrees of freedom for implementing multiple optical functions. In contrast, our complex-amplitude metasurface effectively suppresses phase conjugate replications and diffraction artifacts, while accurately implementing dual focal points with distinct Zernike coefficients to enhance coherent imaging quality. For baseline comparison, we also design and fabricate a phase-only metasurface, which shares the same phase profile as the complex-amplitude metasurface but maintains a unity amplitude profile across the aperture. Figure 2d, e show experimentally captured point spread functions of complex-amplitude and phase-only metasurfaces. The results demonstrate that our complex-amplitude metasurface significantly reduces diffraction artifacts caused by coherent interference between adjacent focal points. To further support this claim, we include additional experiments in Supplementary Fig. 3. These results show that diffraction artifacts from the phase-only metasurface degrade phase retrieval quality, whereas the cleaner intensity profiles enabled by the complex-amplitude metasurface lead to improved reconstruction accuracy and robustness across all reconstruction methods, which is especially beneficial for noise-sensitive applications like ours.

Quantitative phase retrieval with artificial intelligence
The proposed metasurface system can simultaneously capture multiple intensity images with distinct optical aberrations, so that a quantitative phase image can be reconstructed via a phase retrieval algorithm. Conventional phase retrieval algorithms, such as the transport-of-intensity equation (TIE)28, can reconstruct the phase profile ϕ(x,y,z) of a specimen from multiple intensity images captured at different depth planes or with different optical aberrations48. The conventional TIE algorithm is expressed as

k \frac{\partial I}{\partial z} = −\nabla_{xy} \cdot (I\nabla_{xy} \phi)

where I(x,y,z) represents the intensity and k is the wavenumber of the incident light. Despite their widespread use, conventional TIE methods have significant drawbacks, including resolution limitations, susceptibility to noise and artifacts, and difficulties in handling the physical complexities of more compact systems49,50. This makes them less suitable for our metasurface-based system, where coherent wavefront propagation is sensitive to factors including optical aberrations, nanophotonic effects, and nanofabrication imperfections. To overcome these challenges, we develop an AI-driven algorithm that combines physically accurate modeling and AI. The core idea of our approach is to design both a physically accurate microscopy image formation model (forward model) and a phase retrieval algorithm (inverse model), and also to calibrate learnable model components through physics-informed learning and experimentally captured datasets. Due to the absence of publicly available training datasets for QPI and its vulnerability to mismatches between theory and physical systems, relying solely on a single inverse model is insufficient for our applications compared to other applications in holography17,51,52 and computational photography53,54. The forward model enables the simulation of realistic intensity patterns, allowing the inverse model to learn accurate phase retrieval despite optical aberrations and nanoscale defects, providing better robustness and quality. This strategy ensures a deeper understanding of the system’s optical behavior.

The forward model simulates the coherent light propagation through the metasurface microscope system to produce intensity images at specific depth planes as input to the inverse retrieval model. Based on the angular spectrum method55, this model calculates the complex-valued point spread functions (PSFs) of the metasurface system at a particular depth z, which is expressed as

U_z = F^{-1} \{ F \{ U(x,y) \cdot u_{inc} \} \cdot H_z \}

where U(x,y) is the complex-amplitude profile of the metasurface, u_{inc} denotes the incident field, F is the Fourier transform, and H_z is the transfer function for wave propagation at a distance z. The resulting intensity image at depth z can be given by

I_z = | F^{-1} \{ F \{ a_{target} e^{i\phi_{target}} \} \cdot F \{ u_z \} \} |^2 + \eta

where a_{target} and ϕ_{target} denote the target amplitude and phase, and η ∼ N(0,σ^2) is the Gaussian read noise of an image sensor. These intensity images generated by the forward model are crucial for training the inverse model, allowing it to learn accurate mappings from intensity to phase by accounting for the physical system’s behavior.

While conventional TIE-based methods can serve as phase retrieval techniques, they are inadequate for our metasurface QPI system due to their reliance on paraxial approximations, poor handling of high-frequency information, and susceptibility to artifacts from noise and boundary conditions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce an AI-driven inverse model in the form of a convolutional neural network (CNN). Our phase retrieval network, denoted as CNN_{phase}, replaces the conventional TIE by directly converting intensity images into a phase map, bypassing the drawbacks of the traditional approaches. The inverse model can be expressed as

ϕ_{recon} = CNN_{phase}(I_0, I_z)

where I_0 and I_z are intensity images at different depth planes. The network is designed to reconstruct the phase ϕ_{recon}, also compensating for optical aberrations and noise that traditional solvers struggle with (see Supplements for details on training and network architecture). In addition, we augment this inverse model with a secondary correction network, CNN_{corr}, that is trained on experimental datasets to handle discrepancies between our forward model simulations and real-world experimental conditions, including further aberrations, nanofabrication mismatch, and nanoscale system misalignment. By leveraging both forward and inverse models, the system can learn a more accurate representation of the optical system behavior, enhancing the overall phase retrieval process.

Accurate and robust phase retrieval requires a reliable training process. We utilize a physics-informed loss function to guide the learning of our neural networks, ensuring that the reconstructed phase is consistent with the underlying physical principles. Rather than directly comparing phase images, which could lead to ambiguities due to phase offsets, our loss function considers free-space wavefront propagation by evaluating the discrepancies between diffraction patterns at multiple depth planes generated by the reconstructed and target phase maps (ϕ_{target} and ϕ_{recon}):

L(ϕ_{target}, ϕ_{recon}) = \sum_{i} || f_{free}(a_0 e^{i\phi_{target,z_i}}) |^2 - | f_{free}(a_0 e^{i\phi_{recon,z_i}}) |^2 ||^2

where f_{free} represents free-space propagation, z_i is a particular depth for each depth plane i, and a_0 is the amplitude profile at the target plane. By comparing multiple diffraction patterns rather than pixel-wise phase values, this physics-informed loss ensures physical accuracy while improving the network performance and mitigating artifacts like boundary inconsistencies and high-frequency blurring. The training process follows two steps: pre-training with synthetic datasets generated from the forward model, and refinement with experimentally captured datasets. In the pre-training stage, we generate synthetic intensity images using the forward microscopy model, simulating a variety of phase and amplitude distributions under realistic optical conditions, including Gaussian blur and practical constraints on amplitude-phase correlation (see “Methods” for details). This pre-training allows the network to generalize across a wide range of phase objects and handle various aberrations. Once pre-trained, the inverse model is refined with experimental datasets captured from our metasurface system, enabling it to adapt to practical conditions. During the capture refinement, the parameters of the initially trained CNN_{phase} are frozen, and only the parameters of CNN_{corr} are further trained to learn experimental environments. By freezing model parameters after initial pre-training on a large synthetic dataset, we reduce the amount of experimentally captured data required to sufficiently train our inverse model, which is beneficial in this application because both public availability and manual data collection are highly constrained. This approach, incorporating physics-informed learning and training on both synthetic and experimental datasets, enables our model to better understand underlying physical phenomena efficiently, resulting in more accurate, robust learning and superior visual quality compared to conventional methods.

Experimental results
We build an optical microscope setup with our metasurface to compare the performance of our phase retrieval models with existing approaches. The setup includes a coherent laser source with a wavelength of 532 nm, illumination optics, a fabricated metasurface, and a camera. Our metasurface can create two separate intensity images at different depths within a single image plane, allowing the camera to simultaneously capture two images with a single shot. To benchmark our method, we qualitatively and quantitatively assess the retrieved phase image quality and compare several different models: a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)-based direct TIE solver (TIE-Direct) offering fast processing at the cost of limited image quality, an iterative TIE solver (TIE-Iterative) with improved image quality but slow processing time and high sensitivity to optical aberrations, a non-physical inverse model with both physical and learned components but without physics-informed learning (see Supplements for details), and our physics-informed model with physics-informed learning. Note that the non-physical inverse model reflects the type of approach previously explored in deep learning-based QPI studies, which relied on naive forward models without physics-informed supervision or model calibration31,34. While the conventional TIE solvers are fundamentally limited in resolution and sensitive to experimental conditions, inverse models are expected to improve image quality with fast processing time. In particular, physics-informed learning procedures trained on experimental datasets are expected to enhance robustness to optical aberrations, system alignment, and nanofabrication defects, ultimately enabling better imaging performance.

Our initial experiments focus on assessing the performance of CNN_{phase}, initially trained with synthetic datasets generated from the forward microscopy model, using conventional microscopy setups. Figure 4 shows phase retrieval results from the intensity images with various methods. The existing TIE methods provide low image quality and suffer from background noise and artifacts, especially in the low-intensity region, where the solutions tend to diverge (see Supplements for detailed analysis of TIE solvers). In contrast, the inverse models show significant improvements by learning to compensate for aberrations and recover high-frequency details. This demonstrates that our physical modeling approach is effective in overcoming the resolution and robustness limitations of existing TIE methods and improving retrieval quality. In particular, the physics-based supervision enables very high-quality phase reconstruction through additionally supervising physical wave propagation.

Our compact metasurface microscope is composed of the fabricated metasurface with illumination optics and camera. Compared to conventional bulk microscopes, the compact metasurface microscope introduces more challenging conditions, with significantly increased optical aberrations, nanofabrication imperfections, and additional physical phenomena in nanophotonic devices. The correction CNN (CNN_{corr}) in the inverse model is designed to compensate for experiment mismatches and additional artifacts not accounted for in the forward model by refinement training with the experimental dataset captured through our compact metasurface microscope. Figure 5 shows the phase retrieval results, comparing the different inverse models. In all cases, our physics-informed inverse model outperforms baselines by a large margin. Our experimental results on the 1951 USAF resolution target further demonstrate the capability of our microscopy system to resolve element 2 in group 9, corresponding to a nanoscale spatial resolution of 870 nm or better. It is noteworthy that the image quality of the conventional TIE methods and the non-physical model is much worse than that using the conventional microscope in Fig. 4, due to more severe aberrations and additional artifacts caused by simplified design, imperfect nanofabrication, and nanophotonic phenomena of our metasurfaces. This highlights the strength of our approach in achieving robust, accurate phase retrieval even in the presence of complex system imperfections, which conventional methods fail to address, denoting our physics-informed supervision, along with experimental datasets, is inevitable for miniaturization and simplification of microscope systems.

We also demonstrate quantitative validation of our method compared to the others using custom target samples. As a ground truth phase object, we fabricate a custom-designed metasurface target with step-like phase regions defined by 3.10 μm features, equivalent to group 7, element 3 of a standard USAF 1951 target. This target manipulates local phase delay by engineering the effective refractive index of its nanostructures, making it physically equivalent to traditional stepped-height references (see Supplementary Note 3 for details). Figure 5c, d demonstrate that our model can recover quantitative phase information more accurately than other methods (see Supplements for a detailed quantitative comparison of reconstructed phase values). For real-time applications, we also measure the runtime of each method to see how fast our model is compared to others. Our model, with very high performance and robustness, offers fast processing times of 13.5 ms per frame or, similarly, 74 Hz, making it suitable for real-time applications. Notably, our method, based on single-shot measurement, has no additional latency other than computing runtime since the system measures multiple intensity images simultaneously. However, other methods based on multi-shot measurements incur additional time delay between measurements on top of the computational runtime, highlighting the rapid speed of our approach.
